entry.title: The cases that are still waiting
entry.content:
The cases that are still waiting

A reviewer has examined the image and called the person responsible for the property. The call remains unanswered. At the end of the shift, the case is still waiting, but the report wants a result: success, failure or false alarm. Which box should the reviewer choose?

The report is asking for a completed judgment before the service has obtained one. The missing answer belongs to work somebody may still finish. An event the process has no way to handle needs a different intervention. YOJN Care brings these questions together: where did the response stop, and what would let it continue? Tidying the report must not erase the work.

A pending case still holds a question

Until the contact replies, the service can preserve what the reviewer has already established alongside what still needs confirmation. Counting the case as a false alarm makes that missing confirmation disappear; counting it as a completed response makes the service look more effective than the record supports. The pending state needs to carry the question still open and a path through which it might be resolved. It is temporary uncertainty about a particular case, rather than a permanent bin for whatever the reporting system finds inconvenient.

Process noise asks another question: did something happen outside the categories or assumptions used to describe the workflow? That can reveal a missing branch, a failed process or an inadequate model of the operation. A pending confirmation might be resolved through an existing contact path. An event that no branch can describe might require a change to the process itself. Preserving the difference lets the service improve the right thing instead of asking a reviewer to force both into a final label.

A catalogue is a way to examine the design

Work through the combinations of observations and response routes, and the ordinary flow soon branches. An image is incomplete. The owner cannot be reached. A reviewer and a later validator disagree. The event changes while somebody is handling it. A catalogue of such cases asks what the service can know and do at each point, including the paths an ordinary-case diagram might leave out.

The catalogue's value lies in coverage of possibilities. Ten designed cases for one outcome and ten for another can help expose different decisions without implying that the outcomes occur equally often. Those proportions describe how we constructed the catalogue. Field observations would answer the separate question of frequency. Keeping that distinction visible lets the design explore cases freely without turning its assumed distribution into a reported operating rate.

Which cases are we counting?

Some cases reach authorities; some are forwarded to the community as crime; some look suspicious and are later judged otherwise. These groups overlap. A case forwarded as crime and subsequently validated as crime belongs both to the forwarded-crime group and to all completed outcomes. Dividing by either group gives a meaningful fraction, but answers a different question. Cases still awaiting that judgment remain outside both completed groups until an answer arrives.

Examine a case group

Let VV be the number forwarded as crime and validated as crime, CC the number forwarded as crime whose final validation is complete, and NN the number of completed outcomes. Then V/CV/C asks what share of forwarded crime labels agreed with validation; V/NV/N asks what share of all completed outcomes took that confirmed-crime path. The comparison below keeps track of the cases counted in each term.

Comparison Denominator What it asks
Validated crime among completed forwarded-crime cases Forwarded-crime cases with final validation How often did this particular label agree with validation?
The same validated-crime group among completed outcomes All completed outcomes How much of the completed work took this path?
Cases awaiting final validation All recorded events How much recorded work is awaiting final validation?

For unfinished work, let PP count cases awaiting final validation and RR count every recorded event once in the same reporting window. Then P/RP/R gives the pending share. RR includes completed outcomes, pending judgments and unresolved process exceptions; it is not silently replaced by N+PN+P. An exception can still need process repair even when it is not waiting for the particular validation that defines PP.

Understating a crime as suspicion creates a different problem from repeatedly asking people to examine false alarms. Both deserve investigation. Keeping them separate lets the service ask where it missed a serious event and where it created unnecessary work, without expecting one percentage to explain both.

The denominator changes the answer

Imagine a service with 100 recorded events:

State at the reporting time Events Share of all recorded events
Resolved 60 60%
Pending 20 20%
Process exception 20 20%

“Resolved” identifies a completed judgment, not sixty successful responses. Agreement with a later validator could be calculated within those sixty cases, if the relevant judgments exist. It would not describe the other forty. Treating the twenty pending cases as failures would instead turn an unfinished judgment into a final one for the convenience of calculation.

The denominator follows the question. A comparison among completed reviews can describe agreement with validation. A view across all recorded events shows how much remains unresolved and how often the process encountered an exception. Keeping these questions recognisable makes it possible to examine good completed work alongside a growing backlog, instead of allowing one attractive success rate to stand for both.

Where the delay develops

A correct detection can wait in a queue. A reviewer can receive incomplete evidence. A handoff can lose the context needed for the next decision. The last person attached to the case is not necessarily the cause of its delay or outcome. The record needs enough of the sequence to distinguish when the evidence became available, when work was accepted and where the next action stalled. Otherwise the score measures where the case ended up rather than what the person did.

Consider two reviewers in a constructed comparison. One receives a clear view and reaches a judgment quickly. The other receives an old frame, requests a new observation and leaves the case pending. A speed-only ranking rewards the first outcome without describing the different work. A ranking that treats every pending case as incompetence penalises the second reviewer for preserving a question the evidence could not answer. Neither comparison tells us whether a reviewer made good use of what was available. That requires the conditions and the judgment to be examined together.

Look at the pattern before blaming the last person attached to a case. Consistent failure across the service calls for examining its rules; intermittent system-wide failure may point to how work is distributed. Problems across several teams can call for training, while a local cluster may reveal a staffing gap. Individual handling still matters, but it has to be examined within those conditions.

A client's classification may be the agreed operational reference, but it is still a judgment made from a particular position. A later answer may have more context than the reviewer had, or may describe the whole incident while the initial label described one observation. Disagreement can reveal a real mistake, a changed event or a mismatched question. Looking at the evidence available at each point helps distinguish them without making either participant automatically correct.

What a score teaches the reviewer to do

Evaluation changes the work when it becomes an incentive. Suppose completed cases earn a reward while unresolved cases count against a reviewer. That arrangement creates a reason to finalise a label before the missing confirmation arrives. If agreement with a later client judgment is the only rewarded result, guessing the expected answer may become more attractive than describing uncertainty accurately.

Holmström and Milgrom's multitask incentive analysis examines how rewards for measurable work can redirect attention away from other valuable duties that are harder to measure. Its formal model is not a ready-made compensation policy for a response service. The relevant question is what a score encourages the reviewer to neglect. Speed, careful interpretation, context gathering and a reliable handoff can compete for the same attention even though the service needs them together.

Adding more scores does not automatically repair the incentive. A count of evidence requests could reward unnecessary requests. A penalty for disagreement could discourage challenge to a poor reference judgment. The comparison needs an account of good handling before its numbers acquire consequences. Reviewing a sample of completed, pending and disputed cases can help expose what the measures are missing; the review itself needs enough independence and context to avoid simply reproducing the original label.

Accountability remains possible within this richer account. A reviewer can ignore available evidence, leave an accepted task unattended or fail to make a required handoff. Naming the actual failure makes feedback more actionable than a general penalty for a disappointing outcome. It also leaves room for service-level failures to be corrected as service-level failures. Good individual decisions still depend on capacity and recurring work across the service; a performance score cannot supply the missing shift or maintain the equipment carrying the evidence.

A changing service changes the comparison

A revised detector changes which events enter the workflow. A revised procedure can change what a label means. A different staffing arrangement can change handling time. A before-and-after comparison that omits those changes may attribute improvement to the wrong cause, especially if the easier cases enter one period and the difficult cases another. The conditions under which the result was obtained are part of what makes the result interpretable.

The point of evaluation is to make the service easier to understand and improve. A useful account can show a reviewer making a sound judgment, a connection preventing review and an unanswered confirmation in the same operation. Those distinctions keep uncertainty available for work instead of silently converting it into achievement or error. Pending then becomes a question someone can pursue, rather than noise the report learns to hide.

entry.title: The cost of continuing response
entry.content:
The cost of continuing response

An alert can be inexpensive to produce and expensive to resolve. Once a service promises that somebody will examine the event, obtain missing context and carry a response forward, its cost extends beyond the notification. The continuing work is part of the product. If the business model counts only the software transaction, it can make a growing service appear healthier while the people behind it absorb an increasing burden.

YOJN Care’s ambition was a more affordable response service for homes, shops and neighbourhoods, combining detection with human review and community or authorised response routes. Its economics therefore depended on the relationship between monitored sites, customers and the people carrying the queue. More cameras meant more possible evidence sources. More subscriptions meant more commercial commitments. More active events meant more work now. Those counts were connected, but none could substitute for the others in an account of capacity or revenue.

Staffing grows in whole steps

The integrated service models behind Care budgeted one operator per 100 paying Tier 2 customers, rounded up, then one manager per ten operators, also rounded up. These ratios counted paying subscriptions. The handling capacity still depended on when events arrived and how much work each required. At 100 customers the formula gives one operator; at 101 it gives two. At 1,000 it gives ten operators and one manager; at 1,001 it gives eleven operators and two managers.

A model with that shape cannot spread its people costs as though every additional customer buys an infinitesimal fraction of a new shift. Equipment, desks, electricity, connectivity and staff welfare were also part of the design. Purchases associated with additional staff differ from recurring pay and from the use-driven costs of calls or transferred media.

The models also explored public funding and distribution through associations, alongside paying tiers. Those were proposed routes to making coverage affordable, not committed funding or authorised participation by any public body or association. A low subscription price still needed a credible account of who paid for the rest of the operation.

Twenty cases in an hour

Consider an illustrative service receiving twenty cases in an hour, with six minutes of active handling per case. That creates 120 person-minutes of work: the equivalent of two people working continuously for the hour. It says nothing yet about breaks, shift changes, unexpected complexity or the speed at which a new case can begin. Nor does it establish that two people are adequate for the service's response commitments.

The arrival pattern can change the experience without changing the total. Give the toy service two reviewers, assume every case takes exactly six uninterrupted minutes, and omit handoffs and all other work. The contrast is already substantial:

Arrival pattern First cases begin Last case begins Waiting before active handling
All twenty arrive at minute zero Immediately, two at a time Minute 54 Last pair waits 54 minutes
One arrives every three minutes Immediately On its arrival at minute 57 None under these simplified assumptions

Both patterns require 120 person-minutes. In the burst, the reviewers complete ten successive pairs; the last pair cannot start until nine six-minute intervals have passed. The workload total alone says nothing about that wait.

Handling time itself has several forms. Examining an image consumes attention. Waiting for a contact to answer may consume less attention but leaves a case open and creates work when the answer arrives. A handoff may involve two people for part of the interval. Counting every open case as continuous labour overstates one kind of load; counting only button presses erases another. The operation needs to distinguish elapsed case time, active work and the number of cases a person can carry coherently.

Little's queueing result relates long-run average number in a system, arrival rate and time in the system under its conditions. It helps explain how work accumulates. A deadline asks a further question about the distribution of waiting, the response arrangement and the consequences of delay, not only its average.

The next customer may require a whole new step

Some costs grow with use: media transfer, storage, calls or other consumed services. Others arrive in steps. Additional shift coverage requires people even before the new capacity is fully used. A new site may require an installation, device configuration and someone able to maintain it. Additional operating space or equipment creates a different cash requirement from a monthly cloud bill.

This produces a changing relationship between scale and cost. A service with spare capacity may be able to carry more customers without immediately adding a shift. At a capacity boundary, the next group of customers may require a substantial addition. Spreading all costs smoothly across each subscriber can conceal that step. Treating initial equipment and setup as though they recur identically every month creates a different error. A useful economic model distinguishes the work and the timing of the expenditure before averaging it into a unit cost.

Revenue has its own units and timing. An installed site is not necessarily a paying subscriber, and a payer may cover several monitored sources. Acquisition can bring people into the service without converting them into the recurring revenue expected by the model. Cash may arrive after the installation and staffing cost has already been incurred. Growth can improve utilisation while increasing the money needed to keep the service running through the transition.

Acquisition and response are different operations

A distributed partner network can help reach and install more customers. That is a route to acquisition, not an automatic multiplication of response capacity. A partner able to onboard several sites a day may have no role in reviewing their events. If demand is pooled centrally, the shared queue must absorb the new work. If response is local, coverage and escalation need to remain viable in each local operation. Neither arrangement becomes sustainable merely because the onboarding numbers are strong.

The confusion is easy to build into a model. Divide a customer target by the number of customers onboarded per day and the result is a number of days, not operators; manager and salary lines calculated from it cannot show the capacity or surplus their labels suggest. A falling cost per customer needs the same care: a cost worked out for one number of paying users cannot be carried into a column that assumes another.

There is also recurring work between incidents: checking contact details, maintaining equipment, correcting configuration, training people and examining failures. Omitting it from the model treats continuity as free. Moving it to the customer may lower the provider's cost while changing who has to do the work and how dependable the service is. That is a product choice with consequences for use, not just a favourable change in a spreadsheet.

Automation can reduce a specific part of this burden. Better evidence grouping may save repeated review; a reliable routine notification may save manual contact. But a detector that produces more candidate events can increase downstream work even while its computation becomes cheaper. The useful measure is the work required to complete the response at the intended quality, including exceptions, rather than the cost of the automated stage alone.

The economic question is ultimately whether the service can keep its commitment under the conditions in which customers use it. Unfinished reviews still need capacity, and the path carrying their evidence still needs maintenance. A credible model gives that recurring work a place in the cost of continuing. Growth can then be examined for the response the operation can sustain, including the labour and spare capacity on which its promise depends.

entry.title: The evidence path
entry.content:
The evidence path

A device can report that it is connected while the person reviewing an event has no usable image. The network may still carry small messages while struggling with video. The camera may be sending a black frame. A recent upload may contain an old capture. Each situation leaves a different part of the service working and a different question unanswered.

The useful question is whether the reviewer can see enough, soon enough, to decide what to do. A running process cannot answer that. YOJN Care brings the problem into view through four flows between the premises and the reviewer, each carrying something different.

Four signals, four different questions

A heartbeat says the device was reachable. Event metadata says something happened. Images and video let a person examine it. Device and network information help explain a failure. In the figure, A carries heartbeats, B event metadata, C media and D system information. Small heartbeats travel frequently; larger media arrives when an event needs it. They share a connection without answering the same question.

Separating the flows lets a notification arrive before its image. The review allowance can then begin when the image loads, or loading time can be added to it. Either way, waiting for evidence should not consume the time meant for judging it. A failed upload also needs its own investigation; blaming the reviewer will not restore the image.

Several flows share one connection

Imagine a site whose connection has become severely constrained. Small periodic messages still arrive, an alert reaches the queue, and an image upload remains unfinished. Calling the site “online” accurately describes one exchange but conceals the reviewer's situation. Calling it wholly “offline” loses the information still available. A more useful account names what is working: the device was recently reachable, an event was reported, and its supporting media has not yet become available.

This distinction changes the design of degradation. An event notice may need to travel before a large media transfer completes. A smaller preview might support some judgments while a full stream is unavailable; other judgments may remain impossible. Reducing payload or reserving capacity for a control message can help a particular path, but neither creates missing visual detail. The product has to know which decision a degraded view can support, rather than give every delivered artefact the authority of the original evidence.

It also changes diagnosis. Power loss, a disconnected camera, a saturated uplink and an application failure can all produce a missing image. A timeout alone does not identify which happened. The system needs observations along the chain: capture, processing, transfer and presentation. That chain should help someone locate the failure without forcing the reviewer to become a network engineer before they can mark the evidence unavailable.

Delivery is only part of that chain. A camera moved during maintenance may keep streaming while losing the view the review procedure depended on. Poor placement, a noisy feed or a changed reference can leave an image technically available but unhelpful for the intended judgment. Device power and access to the camera source affect whether capture can happen at all. Installation therefore establishes part of the evidence arrangement: what is being observed, through which devices, and who can restore it when the physical setup changes. Network repair alone cannot recover a view that no longer contains the needed scene.

Google's SRE chapter on monitoring distributed systems distinguishes internal instrumentation from checks of externally visible behaviour. For an evidence service, that suggests two complementary questions: do the components appear healthy, and can an authorised review session actually receive a usable result? An end-to-end check can expose a broken path that individual health checks miss. It still needs realistic conditions and cannot establish that every image has the context needed for a human judgment.

How old is this picture?

Suppose a frame was captured before a connection failed, received after reconnection and displayed immediately. For this timeline, take a shared trusted clock:

Event Time Meaning at display
Frame captured 10:00:00 The scene was observed three minutes earlier
Upload received 10:02:58 Transport completed two seconds earlier
Reviewer sees the frame 10:03:00 The presentation is new; the observation is not

An interface showing only “received two seconds ago” invites a different interpretation from “captured three minutes ago.” Keeping both times gives the reviewer the relevant distinction. In a real multi-device path, the clock uncertainty also belongs beside the comparison; apparent precision cannot synchronise the devices by itself.

Age matters in relation to the decision. An older image might help establish how a scene changed, while being insufficient to show what is happening now. A live label cannot carry that judgment on its own. The interface needs to distinguish the latest available capture, a current stream and historical evidence, then make a gap in observation visible. Otherwise a freeze can look like a calm scene, and the absence of new information can acquire a meaning it never earned.

Reconnection brings ordering as well as freshness problems. A delayed alert may arrive after a newer correction. Several attempts to send the same request may all complete. Identifying the event and the relevant change lets the receiver reconcile these messages instead of treating each arrival as a new incident. Where a message initiates an external action, duplicate handling becomes more consequential than duplicate display: retrying the transport should not unknowingly repeat the commitment.

Retrying on a line that is already full

Retries are useful when a failure is transient. They also consume resources. If every device immediately repeats a large transfer during congestion, recovery traffic can compete with the very evidence the service is waiting for. AWS's guidance on limiting retries explains the load created by retries, including compounded attempts across layers, and the role of backoff, jitter and a limit on attempts. Its warning about non-idempotent calls is especially relevant when repeating a request could repeat a side effect.

The service design question is what to recover first. A short message describing the missing evidence may be more immediately useful than another full upload. The latest relevant capture may matter more than an undifferentiated backlog. Historical material may still need retention for review, but it should not crowd out current work by accident. These choices depend on the incident, the available capacity and what the reviewer needs; an indiscriminate “retry until success” policy avoids that judgment rather than solving it.

Moving inference onto a local device changes this path without eliminating it. The device may continue detecting something while disconnected from a remote service. Human review, external notifications and coordinated response may still depend on connections outside it. Local compute can preserve a particular capability through a network interruption, but the product needs to identify that capability precisely. Installation and device maintenance remain part of whether it can continue operating at all.

Care's early Raspberry Pi route brought that operational burden into view. The hardware path was abandoned while installation, device management, manpower and logistics remained unresolved. A later Windows and vendor-software alternative brought recurring costs and integration dependence into the design. The general economic lesson is that a cheap detector can sit inside an expensive delivery arrangement. Provisioning devices, travelling to sites, restoring failures and maintaining compatible integrations all require resources. Comparing the detector's price with a hosted alternative while omitting those responsibilities compares different services. Continuing-response economics needs the whole usable path, including the work that keeps its physical endpoints in place.

What matters is the decision the available evidence can support. If an event is visible but its media is unavailable, the case remains unresolved for a particular reason. The evidence path makes that reason available to the operation: a reviewer can identify what is missing, and the people maintaining the service can investigate where it disappeared. That is more useful than a green or red connection indicator. It connects the state of the system to the work somebody can now do.

entry.title: Who carries the incident?
entry.content:
Who carries the incident?

Imagine a person appearing in a camera frame after a shop's usual hours. The system raises an alert, a neighbour opens it and a monitoring operator receives the same event. Who is carrying it now? The neighbour may assume the operator will act. The operator may be waiting for the owner to explain the scene. The notification has travelled successfully while the responsibility remains between people.

This is the problem behind YOJN Care: how to keep an incident together as different people try to make sense of it and decide what to do. A better detection can help them begin. It cannot tell the next operator what the owner said, whether a neighbour agreed to investigate or who is still waiting for an answer.

An alert needs the knowledge people hold about the scene

The owner might recognise authorised staff where the neighbour sees an unfamiliar person. The operator may have neither person's knowledge. A reference view, the property's instructions and other observations give them something to judge together. The person in the frame has not changed; what they know about that person has.

A personal SOS starts somewhere else. Somebody has deliberately asked for help. They should not need a camera to corroborate the request before it becomes worth attending to. Keeping that origin visible tells the reviewer what question they are answering.

Notifications have to become an incident somebody can follow

Two cameras might show the same person, and each might send several frames as the person moves. Treating every notification as a new case makes more work while scattering the evidence needed to understand any one of them. Group them, and the reviewer can see what changed. A judgment on the first frame can sit beside a later observation still needing attention.

The same context matters when the shift changes. The incoming operator needs the views already examined, the call made to the owner and the unanswered question. Otherwise the handoff merely gives somebody else the job of reconstructing the incident.

The figure combines two kinds of repetition: several cameras observing at once, and one camera observing again. Time, property, camera and classification help decide which notifications belong together. They still need their own judgments. Opening one notification within the incident should make its neighbours available without marking them all as reviewed.

Acknowledgement has a limited meaning

The neighbour has opened the alert. That tells us something, but not whether they can go to the shop. The operator has accepted the review. That does not give them authority to dispatch help. Even when both have responded to the application, the next action may still belong to nobody.

For the shop example, the difference looks like this:

Participant What they have done What remains open
Neighbour Opened the alert and supplied a local observation Has not agreed to respond
Monitoring operator Taken on the review and called the owner Still waiting for the owner's answer
Response participant No acceptance recorded Nobody yet confirmed to take the next action

A useful handoff says which commitment someone has made. “Seen” cannot do the work of “I will continue from here.” Nor can a list of nearby contacts establish that any of them is available.

Time changes the problem, but a timer does not solve it

While the operator waits for the owner, more cases arrive. Some need a quick check; others need a call or an image that has not finished loading. Counting all of that time as neglect would rush necessary work. Letting every active case wait indefinitely would hide the growing queue.

A review clock can make that wait visible and pass a case to someone else. Care's clock example follows the allowances for community, operator and manager review, including time spent loading evidence and making calls. Those are handling windows. They do not measure how long it takes help to arrive.

The next person must also be able to take the case. A manager on a call, an operator on a break and a disconnected workstation cannot absorb the same work as an available responder. And passing a timer's deadline cannot create authority: an escalation to emergency services needs an agreed route and their participation.

A quiet screen can mean several different things

Suppose the operator has judged the scene suspicious. Another frame may show the person leaving, or reveal something more serious. Continuing to record matters. Asking the operator to repeat the same judgment for every frame may not.

That leaves two separate choices: whether to keep the observation, and whether to ask for attention again. Silence alone tells the next operator neither. The camera might still be recording while repeated alerts are suppressed. Another person might have taken over the watch. Or the connection might have failed.

Care's crime-classification rule illustrates the distinction: later notifications could keep joining the incident while further processing was suppressed for two hours. Suspicion had no equivalent cooldown because it could develop into crime. These choices make sense only if the person watching can tell which rule applies. A quiet screen must not look like evidence that the shop is safe.

The outcome can exceed the application's account

The owner might call the police directly. A responder might arrive without updating the interface. An absent update then means the application does not know, rather than that nothing happened. The reverse error is just as consequential: a recorded request does not establish arrival or resolution. An unanswered question needs to remain available for someone to pursue.

Return to the shop at the change of shift. The incoming operator has two views, knows why the owner was called and can see that an answer is still due. They know who has offered to help and what remains unassigned. That is something they can continue. Without it, the system may keep delivering every alert correctly while everyone waits for somebody else.

entry.title: A precognition court for AI
entry.content:
A precognition court for AI

Imagine an AI powerful enough to rewrite its own programming. We have given it rules intended to keep it safe. What stops it from changing those too?

That was the question behind my January 2024 thought experiment. If the safeguards live entirely inside the system they constrain, we are asking the actor to preserve the rules against which it will be judged. I wanted to put those rules somewhere it could consult but could not unilaterally rewrite. Blockchain interested me as one possible way to make that separation difficult to undo: a shared account maintained outside the AI, with the AI excluded from control of its consensus mechanism.

The ambition was a fail-safe. The thought experiment is how to build one, not evidence that a blockchain has already made an AI safe.

First, it is a ledger

You can keep a ledger on paper, in a spreadsheet or in a database. A blockchain is another way of keeping a record, with a protocol through which participants agree on its history. The interesting part here is what it would take for one participant to change a record that others rely on.

Bitcoin's proof-of-work design makes a changed block require new work, including work for the blocks following it. Its security argument assumes that honest participants collectively control more computational power than the attacker. Under that assumption, an attacker's chance of catching up falls as confirmations accumulate.1 That is a conditional, costly-to-rewrite record, not an infinitely difficult problem. Adding participants alone does not make a network invulnerable. Other consensus designs use different resources and assumptions; Ethereum's proof-of-stake documentation, for example, describes attacks and recovery involving both stake and social coordination.2

The attraction remains: a powerful program should have to contend with an independently maintained system rather than edit a local file and declare itself exempt. But the independence has to exist in the actual arrangement. A chain controlled by the same actor would give the proposal an impressive name without the separation it needs.

Ball is in your court now

Suppose the rules are outside the acting AI. My January 2024 proposal went as far as every atomic action: before taking any such action, the AI would submit it to a service that checks it against those rules. Permission or refusal would return before the action proceeds. The decision and the version of the rules used would enter the shared record.

Note

A universal ambition. Checking every atomic action was the proposed scope, not a demonstrated capability. Defining the unit of action, checking it quickly enough and dealing with consequences the checker cannot predict remain feasibility questions.

Call it the Precognition Court: the court is supposed to act before the consequence, rather than merely explain it afterwards.

The checking service would be automated but would not itself depend on another AI making an open-ended judgment. It would assess requests, identify patterns among refused actions and feed those patterns into a reward mechanism. Earning that reward would be part of the acting AI's objective, so the system would learn to stay within the rules rather than repeatedly collide with them.

There are two different jobs in that proposal. The check decides whether this action may proceed under the current rule. Learning is intended to make future behaviour better. A reward for compliance cannot replace the check: the action still has to meet the rule even while the system is learning. The proposal needs a way to express the action, evaluate it and handle what the checker cannot determine. Those are substantial parts of the problem.

Separation of church and state

Asimov's laws offer a familiar image of rules above an individual machine's preferences. The harder question is how those rules acquire enough meaning to govern a real situation, and how they improve when a case exposes a mistake.

AI researchers cannot answer that alone. The court would bring people from public policy, medicine, social science, psychology, defence and other disciplines into governing the rules. They understand different consequences of an action. The acting system would be a citizen of that arrangement, subject to its laws rather than free to change them whenever they obstructed its purpose.

The record of requests and decisions would give those people something to examine. Repeated refusals could reveal a harmful strategy, a badly described request or a rule blocking a legitimate need. They would have to distinguish those possibilities, investigate consequences and amend the rule deliberately. The record supplies cases; it does not supply the answer to every case.

That is why keeping the AI outside the voting mechanism matters to the idea. It separates producing an action from deciding the rules under which the action is permitted. The people changing the rules still need a mandate, and the people affected need a way to question them. A technically independent court could otherwise concentrate all the consequential choices in another unaccountable institution.

The rule has to reach the action

My proposed hardwiring went as far as dedicated circuitry integrated into each deployed AI, routing every command that reached it through the external check and back before continuing. It was meant to make the court compulsory for every atomic action, rather than another instruction the AI could choose to ignore. Ensuring that no action could bypass such a circuit remained part of the problem.

A smaller, invented example helps expose what that requirement means. A document service prepares a report and obtains approval for version one. It then changes a passage before release. The earlier decision does not automatically approve version two. The release tool has to examine the version actually being sent and the decision that applies to it. If the service also holds an unrestricted upload credential, it can bypass the court altogether.

The path from approval to effect therefore matters as much as the record of approval. A common ledger can make an altered account harder to conceal. It cannot, merely by existing, stop an action occurring through a route outside the arrangement. Keeping the rule beyond the actor's control and making the action depend on that rule are connected engineering problems.

A court people can question

Now suppose the report contains an error, but the court's rules describe only an initial release. The author wants to correct it; a reader needs to know which version to rely on; the operator needs a procedure it can carry out. A refusal may be faithful to the rule while revealing that the rule is incomplete.

Who can bring that case? Who can inspect the reasons for the refusal? Who may amend the policy? A useful court needs answers that do not depend entirely on the organisation whose decision is being challenged. Different kinds of expertise help, but expertise and the right to decide for other people are not the same thing.

A revised policy could distinguish a correction from a new release, identify when it takes effect and preserve the earlier decision in the history. An urgent correction might need a quicker path than a general change to the rules. That path still needs a visible scope; otherwise exceptions become a second policy known only to the operators. The aim is to make a mistaken rule correctable without giving the acting system an unrestricted escape from review.

This is the wider possibility that made decentralisation interesting to me: people improving a shared arrangement while the system governed by it cannot simply remove the constraints. Recording votes or allocating tokens does not by itself settle who should govern. The question is what the participants can understand, contest and change, and whether their judgment reaches the action.

The helmet

When I first wrote this, I did not expect a rogue AGI any time soon. Relax! This is just a fun thought experiment. The engineering difficulties do not make the question uninteresting. They tell us what the proposed fail-safe would have to survive: a changed rule, a mistaken judgment, an attacker and an action trying to leave through another door.

My uncle's advice was simpler: you do not need a helmet every day; you need it on the day you have an accident. You do not know which day that will be, so put it on.

That is the spirit of the court. Think about the restraint before the accident, and make sure it is attached to something that can actually restrain the action.

For a more grounded view of the state of AI, there is The autocorrect paradox.

  1. Satoshi Nakamoto, Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System, sections 4 and 11. The attack analysis depends on relative computational power and accumulated work. ↩

  2. Ethereum's proof-of-stake attack and defence documentation explains the different assumptions and the role of social coordination in some recoveries. Proof of work is not a description of every blockchain. ↩

entry.title: When an approval reaches the effect
entry.content:
When an approval reaches the effect

A report has been reviewed and approved. Before release, the document service that prepared it changes a passage to answer an objection. Does the earlier approval still apply? A record saying only “approved” leaves the next participant to invent the answer.

The useful decision identifies the document, the permitted use and the version the person examined. The release path can then compare what it is about to do with what was accepted. This is where an independent judgment meets the machinery that carries its consequence. Across a network of reused AI capabilities, the kind DAOnet’s design describes, that connection would let a contributor and a receiving team coordinate an actual use, rather than rely on a catalogue entry’s general promise.

The version travels with the decision

The relationship is small enough to state explicitly:

Step in the hypothetical release Object that must remain identifiable
Propose the document The particular document version and intended use
Review and decide The reviewer, decision scope and version examined
Attempt the release The actual version presented to the release path
Record the result What was permitted or refused, and whether the release occurred

Approval of version one does not answer the request to release version two. The release path needs to compare them and return the changed work for a relevant decision. An independent record makes an invented approval harder to conceal; a constrained release path makes bypassing the decision harder. A faithful record cannot stop an unrestricted upload credential, while a gate checking an untrustworthy assertion can enforce the wrong decision efficiently.

A decision to permit the release is also different from the release happening. The tool may fail, the destination may be unavailable or the attempt may stop before the document becomes accessible. Recording only the permission would leave the participants without an account of the consequence they were trying to govern.

An article makes the same distinction familiar. Its author corrects a paragraph after review; the publisher now has different words to examine. Gazette can build the corrected page, but a successful build cannot accept the new paragraph on the publisher’s behalf. The writing, its rendered page and the decision to release it each need to remain identifiable.

YojnAI’s proposed improvement workflow put a similar distinction inside the application: feedback on a trace, a candidate improvement job, inspection of its result and an explicit push of a chosen version were separate steps. A one-click return to an earlier version belonged to that deployment design. By contrast, a partner application’s trace service could update feedback on an event row; changing that assessment was not itself a decision to deploy different application behaviour. Choosing a version needs the link from reviewed evidence to the actual effect.

Another route can undo the arrangement

Suppose the release tool faithfully rejects the changed document, but the service also holds an unrestricted credential to upload it directly. The court that judges an action before it happens has examined the request without governing the consequence. The second route has to be brought into the arrangement or removed before the judgment can do its intended work.

Another actor able to replace the document afterwards creates a related dependency. Following those routes tells us where the control actually reaches and where somebody else's responsibility begins. A common record can make a departure visible; the path carrying the action gives the decision its practical force.

The same question applies to an urgent correction. A process can provide a narrow route for it without making every release depend on a general policy amendment. That route still needs an identifiable decision, a scope and an account of the resulting version. Otherwise the exception becomes an alternative publication path with fewer constraints, rather than a way to handle the specific need.

What the shared account contributes

The statements entering the common record still depend on their sources. If one participant asserts that a document was approved, the record needs a way to identify the approving party and the decision's scope. If a physical event happened outside the system, a ledger entry cannot manufacture observation of it. Agreement about a recorded statement and evidence for the event are connected but different parts of the arrangement.

This helps make the architectural choice more precise. Which disagreement does the shared mechanism resolve? Is the concern an operator altering records, participants seeing incompatible versions or a single organisation controlling access? Signed records or a shared database may answer the particular problem more simply. A new chain also requires adoption, infrastructure and a way to handle its own failures.

The document service makes the ambition concrete. A particular version meets a decision, that decision governs a release and the resulting record lets participants examine whether the consequence matched what was accepted. A shared mechanism earns its place if it makes this relationship more dependable across the people involved. The useful achievement is a consequence connected to accountable judgment, with a record people can use to understand and contest it.

entry.title: Some things never change. It’s time they do…
entry.content:
Some things never change. It’s time they do…

Okay. Before we get into AI interoperability and the possible role of a blockchain, a refresher.

What is a blockchain? In its most rudimentary form, a ledger. A better one, or a worse one, depending on the use case. Cryptography helps participants verify records; a consensus mechanism determines which history they accept. The familiar operations of creating, reading, updating and deleting data take a different shape when participants need to agree on a shared record. “Immutable” is shorthand for resistance to rewriting under the system's security assumptions, not a magical exemption from attack.1 Once you have that ledger, you can do cool shit with it. DeFi was all the craze a couple of years before I wrote this in May 2024.

And a neural network? At this level of abstraction, a function approximator. Think of a sine wave and the periodic functions it suggests; then think of aperiodic, linear and nonlinear relationships. Given data spread through an n-dimensional space, can a network learn a useful relationship among the values? Fitting those examples is one part. Generalising beyond them is what makes the result useful. I hear “generation” is all the craze these days.

Cool. That's it. No more extra-credit assignments from this point on.

I lied. There's one more thing.

What's an API? A defined way for software systems to talk to each other. A really awesome one, sometimes. Its usefulness depends on what it lets the other system do.

The interface stayed familiar

Software had decades in which to develop its routines, interfaces, deployment practices and containers. Then the post-2022 AI rush made a familiar neighbourhood model, GPT, everyone's business. The question I was asking in 2024 was what happened when we took established software interfaces and translated them almost verbatim into this much younger wave of applications.

Did you read the paragraph above?

Yes or no?

That gives us a simple state to reason about. In an ordinary program, we can often name routines, describe their inputs and outputs, and expose the parts another program needs to call. For a fixed set of inputs and state, a deterministic routine produces a fixed result. Randomness and concurrency can complicate that behaviour, while the named routines still give us parts to examine and compose.

A trained neural network offers a different problem. We can see its architecture and, where available, its parameters. That does not automatically give us a set of independent, named abilities that can be lifted out and used like ordinary routines. Knowing where multiplication occurs is not the same as knowing where “understands a supplier's exception” lives.

Yet the familiar request-and-response interface is often the first thing we build around it. That is useful. It can also conceal the part we have not learned how to separate.

Consider Docker and the software engineering practices around containers. They arrived through years of testing, adoption and adjustment. The AI application rush was trying to compress a comparable maturation into a couple of years. Two years versus decades. What could go wrong?

Plenty.

Zero or one: which part can another system call?

A modern AI application can look remarkably like an operating system, loosely speaking. Retrieval is part of its input/output path. Context resembles working memory. Agents resemble threads carrying out activities. These are analogies, not literal descriptions of an LLM's internals, but they help locate the work.

A model is invoked at a particular point in the agent flow. The orchestration framework supplies context, remembers intermediate results, chooses the next call and eventually returns an answer. Much of the application's useful behaviour lives in that arrangement around the model.

Now let a second system call it. Suppose the exposed choices are only:

  • Zero: call the base language model.
  • One: call the complete orchestrated application and receive its final answer.

Calling that final endpoint from an ordinary application may be entirely sufficient. But when one agent system needs to work with another, the choice is limiting. It may need the state reached halfway through a task, the evidence already collected, or a callback when a particular agent has finished. Starting again at the base model discards useful work. Calling the final endpoint asks for more work than the receiving system needs.

The problem is not that an API is incapable of carrying state. An application can persist memory and expose finer operations. The problem is that a wrapper which exposes only those two endpoints has not done so. Its caller cannot reach the internal memory merely because the application uses agents. And exposing that memory still says nothing about whether learned abilities inside the underlying model are independently reusable.

What we tried with YojnAI

With YojnAI, our approach was to wrap memory states in a data structure and keep caching those states so the application could expose callbacks at the agent level. A caller could work with an intermediate state instead of choosing only between the base model and the final orchestration endpoint.

This also let us “teach” the invoked LLMs to work with the wrapper's memory operations during the application flow. The wrapper kept the states; the model could use those operations. That is different from a neural network acquiring a memory subsystem we could lift out and transplant into another model.

We built utilities on top of that work and called them Apps. Different story. YojnAI's application design follows those parts through the work a customer needed to do.

But even that approach was not enough for the larger question.

A third possibility: combine the learned parts

What I really wanted was a third scenario: a subnet of one neural network working with a subnet of another. Not merely their final answers passing through an endpoint. The learned capacities themselves becoming composable.

Imagine a model M1 containing capacities I1, I2, I3, …, In, realised through subnets which might overlap. Another model, M2, contains capacities K1, K2, K3, …, Kn, again potentially overlapping.

How would you take K2 from M2, and I2 and I3 from M1, to make M3?

Note

Naming a capacity does not isolate it. The notation makes the question easy to write. It does not establish that those capacities are cleanly located, separable or compatible. Overlap is part of the difficulty. Removing the part we call I2 might also remove something I3 relies on. Two representations that work within their own models may not mean the same thing when connected.

There are two different times at which we might attempt the combination:

When the combination happens The question it raises
Before deployment, loosely like compilation Can selected learned components be aligned and assembled into a new model which preserves the wanted capacities?
During execution, loosely like runtime linking Can one running system use a selected learned capacity in another, with the representations, state and dependencies needed for that interaction?

Pre-deployment composition is a research problem of its own. Work such as Git Re-Basin examines a particular route to aligning and merging model weights.2 The runtime question reaches beyond what a request-and-response wrapper has solved. Transporting a message cannot, by itself, discover a decomposition of the learned computation or make incompatible representations fit.

That was the force of my complaint about the API model. The familiar interface can carry the eventual interaction. It cannot substitute for understanding what is being composed.

My gut said a blockchain might have a role here. A shared record could help parties coordinate contributions, versions or use. It would still need something meaningful to record. The road from a ledger to a working M3 is long and hard.

The inquiry continues in The intelligence between the parts. It asks what must pass between learned capacities for their combination to retain meaning. There is also nearer work we can do without claiming to have solved that problem: make the capabilities we already know how to share intelligible to their next user.

Several different things can look like intelligence

A model, a prompt, a dataset, a workflow and a hosted service can each contribute to a useful result, but the next team receives something different in each case. A dataset provides examples, a prompt supplies instructions in a context and a workflow connects operations. A model contains learned parameters, while an endpoint offers a response with much of its implementation remaining at the provider. These forms carry different dependencies and different opportunities to change the behaviour: adopting a prompt leaves the consumer to supply the model and its context, whereas invoking a service leaves more of the operation with the provider. A useful catalogue makes that contribution and continuing responsibility intelligible, so a team can discover the form it actually needs.

Application composition is a nearer form of reuse

Consider two hypothetical document capabilities. One extracts supplier details from an invoice; another checks a proposed payment against the extracted terms. They can be combined through defined inputs and outputs. The second does not need the first system's entire internal process, but it does need enough context to know what the result means. Was the supplier identity confirmed or merely inferred? Is a payment date absent, or was extraction unsuccessful? Does the returned value refer to this invoice or another record? Each distinction changes what the checking step can do with the answer.

A catalogue entry for that invented extraction capability could carry a compact account rather than a promise of general document understanding:

Part of the capability description Example declaration
Object being supplied A document-extraction workflow, not a trained subnetwork
Input A declared family of invoice documents
Output Supplier fields and payment terms, with source locations and unresolved values
Required context Document identity, language and the selected workflow version
Evaluation question Whether supported examples preserve the fields and evidence needed by the payment check
Boundary No authority to approve or execute a payment
Conditions of use The workflow's licence and dependencies, without any customer's invoice data

The next component can now ask a particular question of the output. An absent payment date can remain unresolved rather than masquerade as a zero or an extraction success. Another document layout gives the receiving team a case to test, not a reason to assume the same result. The description supplies a starting point for adoption; the receiving application still has to examine the contribution in its own setting.

Versioning is a relationship with downstream work

If the extraction changes, the checking step may change even when its own code does not. A newer model might recognise more layouts and produce a different format. A revised tool might treat a missing field differently. Moving from a source location to a bare value could leave the payment check without the evidence it used to receive. Versioning connects those changes to the downstream work that depends on them; its value comes from identifying relevant behaviour and requirements.

The application needs to identify which capability it used and retain enough context to investigate a regression. Keeping an earlier configuration available can support recovery, provided its dependencies can still be supplied. The practical promise of reuse is less repeated work. Unannounced changes reverse that promise when every consumer has to rediscover the same failure, reconstruct its cause and repair their application separately.

Adoption gives the description a test

The receiving team can now try the capability against a small set of its own permitted documents. Some may match the declared layout; one may use a different currency convention; another may omit a term that the payment check requires. This is where the description becomes useful. It tells the team which result would count as a supported contribution, which case should return an unresolved value and which case needs another adapter or method.

A failed adoption can improve the shared account. If the consumer had supplied a supported document and lost its source locations, the implementation may need correction. If the document was outside the declared family, a clearer discovery filter could have saved the trial. If the output was faithful but the consumer needed a different question answered, the capability may be working and still be the wrong choice. A network that retains those distinctions can improve discovery without turning every poor fit into a bad rating.

This form of adoption is already a useful contribution to the larger ambition. A catalogue can make models, workflows and methods easier to adopt while keeping clear which object is being shared.

Rights travel with the dependency

A useful configuration may contain a customer's process. A model may carry a licence with particular limits. A dataset may be available for one purpose without permission for another. A standard interface can connect them while their rights remain different. The consumer needs to know which contribution they may use, how they may change it and what must stay with the original owner.

DAO Studio's platform and partner-product distinction made this concrete: the shared platform and the application made for a partner could have different owners. A reusable mechanism could emerge from service work while the partner's records and particular work remained theirs. That boundary makes a contribution possible without asking people to surrender everything they bring. It also gives the receiving team a clearer account of what they can build upon.

What a network would have to add

A functioning capability may already be useful to one organisation. A network would need to make something else easier: discovery, comparison, composition, payment, coordination or maintaining a shared account of versions. Contributors need demand; users need capabilities worth adopting. A useful protocol connects those needs to work people can already value, with a reason to participate beyond the hope of a larger network.

DAOnet explored that protocol ambition through a proposed ledger, memory, observation and execution stack for agents. The wider goal was cumulative capability: one team’s work becoming a useful contribution to another application. A common record could support part of the coordination, while a catalogue and intelligible interfaces could support others. The choice of mechanism should follow the interaction it improves.

Useful work can accumulate only if its conditions remain intelligible as it travels. A shared capability should save the next person from repeating the mechanism, not force them to repeat the investigation into what it actually means.

  1. Nakamoto's Bitcoin paper states the honest computational-majority assumption behind its history-selection argument. Other consensus systems have their own assumptions; the ledger description here does not make them interchangeable. ↩

  2. Ainsworth, Hayase and Srinivasa, Git Re-Basin: Merging Models modulo Permutation Symmetries, studies aligning model units through permutations and merging in weight space. It is a specific model-merging result, not the arbitrary I/K-capacity operation posed here. ↩
